ai.definition: Post-Quantum Cryptographic Shields refer to encryption methods designed to be secure against potential future attacks from advanced quantum computing technologies, which can break many of the current public-key cryptography systems.
ai.howItWorks: These shields employ lattice-based and code-based cryptographic algorithms. Lattice-based cryptography uses mathematical lattices in high dimensions for security, while code-based cryptography relies on the hardness of decoding a general linear code to provide security against quantum attacks.
ai.problemSolved: The primary problem addressed is ensuring long-term data security in an era where classical encryption methods may become vulnerable due to advancements in quantum computing capabilities.
ai.manufacturing: Manufacturing involves developing and testing new cryptographic algorithms, which requires significant computational resources for simulation and validation. It also includes the development of hardware that can efficiently implement these algorithms.
ai.buildProcess: The build process starts with theoretical research and algorithm design, followed by rigorous mathematical proofs and empirical testing to ensure security against both classical and quantum attacks. This is then translated into practical implementations and tested in real-world scenarios.
ai.costDrivers: Cost drivers include the high computational resources required for initial development, extensive validation processes, and potential hardware costs associated with implementing these algorithms efficiently.
ai.lifecycleOutlook: The outlook is positive as there is a growing recognition of the need for post-quantum security, but widespread adoption is still in its early stages due to the complexity and cost involved.
ai.regulation: Regulatory frameworks are beginning to emerge, but standards and guidelines are not yet fully established. There is a push from both government bodies and industry groups to develop and implement these standards.
ai.risks: Risks include the potential for breakthroughs in quantum computing that could render current post-quantum algorithms insecure before they can be widely deployed, as well as the complexity of integrating new cryptographic methods into existing systems.
ai.profitability: Profitability is uncertain due to the high initial investment required and the long-term nature of the technology. However, once established, it has the potential for significant market value in sectors requiring robust security measures.
ai.futureDevelopment: Future development will likely focus on refining algorithms, improving efficiency, and developing new protocols that can be seamlessly integrated into existing infrastructure.
ai.energyRequirements: Field units draw low hundreds of watts; fabrication is energy-intensive due to vacuum baking. Algorithm implementation requires significant computational resources but does not have high power consumption.

glossary.def: A cryptographic system that uses the hardness of problems related to mathematical lattices for security.
A type of post-quantum cryptography based on the difficulty of decoding a general linear code.

subsystems.name: Algorithm suite
subsystems.role: the mathematical core — encryption, key exchange and signatures that resist quantum attack.

subsystems.name: Key management
subsystems.role: generate, store, rotate and revoke keys, including hybrid keys.

subsystems.name: Protocol integration
subsystems.role: slot the new algorithms into the internet's existing handshakes and tunnels.

subsystems.name: Hardware and performance
subsystems.role: make the maths fast enough for real traffic, from servers to smart cards.

subsystems.name: Migration and hybrid mode
subsystems.role: run classical and post-quantum algorithms together so that a break in either does not expose traffic.

subsystems.name: Assurance and testing
subsystems.role: prove implementations match the standard and are free of side channels.

buildSteps.title: Pick hard problems
buildSteps.detail: Cryptographers identify mathematical problems believed hard even for quantum computers, such as finding short vectors in high-dimensional lattices or decoding random linear codes.

buildSteps.title: Design algorithms
buildSteps.detail: From those problems, they build encryption, key-exchange and signature schemes with concrete parameter sizes.

buildSteps.title: Public cryptanalysis
buildSteps.detail: The designs are published and attacked by the global research community for years to find weaknesses.

buildSteps.title: Standardise
buildSteps.detail: Standards bodies such as NIST select algorithms and publish formal specifications; its first post-quantum standards (FIPS 203, 204 and 205) appeared in 2024.

buildSteps.title: Implement efficiently
buildSteps.detail: Engineers write reference code, then optimise it for CPUs, GPUs and constrained devices, checking for timing leaks.

buildSteps.title: Integrate into protocols
buildSteps.detail: The new primitives are added to TLS, SSH, VPNs and certificate systems, often as hybrid options alongside classical algorithms.

buildSteps.title: Test and validate
buildSteps.detail: Implementations are checked against test vectors and formally verified where possible.

buildSteps.title: Deploy and migrate
buildSteps.detail: Organisations inventory long-lived secrets, enable hybrid mode, then phase out RSA and elliptic-curve cryptography.

prerequisites.why: lattice and code problems are believed hard for both classical and quantum computers, though not proven.
NIST completed a multi-year competition and published the first standards in 2024.
optimised libraries for lattice arithmetic already run on common CPUs.
some CPUs and hardware security modules have added support, but many devices still run software only.
many systems hard-code algorithms, making swaps slow and risky.
certificate authorities and key stores must issue and manage the new certificate types.

pathway.milestone: NIST standards published in 2024; browsers and cloud providers testing hybrid key exchange.
pathway.unlocks: early protection for today's encrypted traffic against future quantum decryption.

pathway.milestone: Widespread hybrid deployment in TLS, VPNs and messaging; certificate authorities begin issuing post-quantum certificates.
pathway.unlocks: confidence that no single algorithm failure breaks security.

pathway.milestone: Full migration for long-lived data and critical infrastructure; classical-only systems phased out.
pathway.unlocks: protection of data that must stay secret for decades.

pathway.milestone: Cryptographic agility becomes routine, allowing quick swaps if weaknesses are found.
